module_title: Tenure Holders, Tribal Protections, and Boundaries
introduction: This intermediate tier dissects who actually 'owns' the land. It explains the specific classes of tenure holders under the UP and MP Codes, the strict statutory protections preventing the exploitation of Dalit and Tribal farmers, and the resolution of boundary disputes.

core_concepts.title: State Ownership of All Lands
core_concepts.description: Under modern codes (Sec 57 MPLRC), all lands belong to the State Government. Farmers are not absolute sovereign owners; they are 'Tenure Holders' holding the land *under* the State, subject to the payment of land revenue.

core_concepts.title: Classes of Tenure Holders (UP Revenue Code, Sec 74)
core_concepts.description:
The UP Code simplified dozens of old complex tenancies into four clean categories:
1. Bhumidhar with Transferable Rights (BTR): The highest class. Permanent, heritable, and freely transferable interest.
2. Bhumidhar with Non-Transferable Rights (BNTR): Permanent and heritable, but CANNOT be sold or transferred. (Usually land allotted by the government to landless persons). After a statutory period (e.g., 5/10 years), BNTR upgrades to BTR.
3. Asami: A minor, temporary tenant holding land from a Bhumidhar or the Gram Panchayat.
4. Government Lessee: Holds land under specific lease terms with the government.

core_concepts.title: Bhoomiswami (MP Land Revenue Code, Sec 158)
core_concepts.description: The equivalent of the BTR in Madhya Pradesh. A *Bhoomiswami* holds the highest form of agricultural tenancy in MP, possessing permanent, heritable, and transferable rights in the land.

core_concepts.title: Restrictions on Transfer (Protecting Marginalized Communities)
core_concepts.description:
To prevent wealthy landlords from exploiting poor farmers, Codes strictly restrict land transfers.
- UP Code (Sec 98): A Bhumidhar belonging to a Scheduled Caste (SC) CANNOT transfer their land by sale, gift, or lease to a non-SC person WITHOUT the prior written permission of the Collector.
- MPLRC (Sec 165): A Bhoomiswami belonging to an Aboriginal Tribe (ST) is completely barred from transferring land to a non-tribal person in notified areas, ensuring tribal lands remain within the community.

important_entities.name: Demarcation & Boundary Disputes
important_entities.key_fact: Resolved by the Sub-Divisional Officer (SDO) or Tahsildar.
important_entities.significance: When two farmers fight over the exact boundary of their adjacent fields, they do not go to a Civil Court. They file an application for Demarcation (Sec 24 UP Code / Sec 129 MPLRC). The Revenue Inspector maps the land using fixed survey marks and physical measurements, and the Tahsildar/SDO settles the physical boundary.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Can a Bhumidhar with Non-Transferable Rights (BNTR) leave their land to their nephew through a Will (Bequest)? **NO**. Because a BNTR has strictly non-transferable rights, any Will executed by them regarding that specific land is completely void. The land will devolve strictly according to the statutory rules of succession.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: B B A G (BTR, BNTR, Asami, Government Lessee)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use BBAG to quickly recall the four exclusive classes of tenure holders established by the UP Revenue Code 2006 [1.1.1].

exam_strategy_tips: In UP PCS-J Mains, if asked about Dalit land rights, explicitly cite **Section 98 of the UP Revenue Code, 2006**, explaining it as a socio-economic shield requiring the Collector's prior approval for SC to non-SC land transfers.
